title: Prepare-and-measure quantum key distribution from a bound on information leakage
authors: Abhishek Mishra, Michele Masini, Maria Balanzó-Juandó, Armin Tavakoli, Stefano Pironio
abstract: Every quantum key distribution (QKD) protocol must limit the information available outside the users' laboratories. In device-independent QKD this is essentially the only assumption made on the devices. In a prepare-and-measure setting it cannot be imposed strictly, since the sender's device must emit a signal that depends on her private input. The natural replacement, and a minimal one, is a leakage bound: a bound on how much information about the input leaves the sender's laboratory, through the intended signal or through any side channel. We ask how far this unavoidable requirement can replace a detailed model of the source. We show that this single bound, quantified by the probability of guessing the input from everything the source emits, suffices to prove security against collective attacks. In our analysis, nothing is assumed about the precise form of the emitted states, their dimension, energy or purity, nor about the receiver's measurement device, beyond the standard requirement that it does not leak Bob's data. The standard B92 and BB84 protocols do not certify any key under this minimal leakage bound assumption. But closely related protocols can and, in the ideal limit, achieve one secret bit per key round. For noisy implementations, we compute key rates using semidefinite programming relaxations. Our best protocols tolerate visibilities down to 0.84, corresponding to an 8% quantum bit error rate, compared with the 11% threshold of standard device-dependent BB84.
summary: This paper develops a security framework for Prepare-and-Measure QKD by introducing a minimal 'leakage bound' assumption, which quantifies the maximum information about the key input that can leak from the source. It proves this single bound is sufficient to guarantee security against collective attacks, leading to improved key rate estimates compared to standard protocols.
main_problem: The paper addresses the security analysis of Prepare-and-Measure Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) protocols by replacing the need for detailed source modeling with a minimal assumption: a leakage bound (LB).
main_result: The leakage bound assumption is shown to be sufficient to prove security against collective attacks, and the best analyzed protocols can tolerate visibilities down to 0.84, outperforming standard BB84 thresholds.
method: The analysis uses information theory bounds, semidefinite programming (SDP) relaxations, and the quantification of the optimal guessing probability ($P_{g,n}$) to establish security criteria.
model_or_system: The model is the P&M QKD setting, involving Alice's source emitting states $ho_{QE0}^x$, Eve's interaction, and Bob's measurement device. Security is assessed by bounding the information leakage about the input $x$.
key_observables: Key rate ($K_\infty$), Guessing Probability ($P_{g,n}$), Conditional von Neumann Entropy ($H(A|E\Theta)$), and the leakage bound constant ($G$).
important_parameters: Visibility ($v$), Quantum Bit Error Rate (QBER), and the leakage bound constant $G$.
main_assumptions: The core assumption is the leakage bound $P_{g,n}\{ho_{QE0}^x\} \le G$, which is minimal and does not require assumptions on the precise form or purity of the emitted states.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the P&M QKD process flow involving Alice's source, Eve's eavesdropping isometry, and Bob's measurement.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the necessity of the leakage bound (LB) as a replacement for full source modeling. It then proves that this single bound is sufficient for security against collective attacks, deriving key rate formulas using SDP relaxations and comparing results against standard protocols.
why_interesting: The work provides a rigorous, minimal security framework for QKD that is applicable even when the physical source characteristics are unknown, which is highly relevant for practical quantum communication implementations.
